Read it from the innermost node outward, and compare the planner's estimated row counts against the actual ones. A large divergence between estimate and actual is the single most common root cause, and it usually points at stale statistics or a correlation the planner cannot see.

Then look for the specific antipatterns. Sequential scans on large tables suggest a missing index or a predicate the index cannot serve, such as a function wrapped around the indexed column. Nested loop joins over large row counts suggest the planner underestimated cardinality. High buffer reads relative to rows returned mean the query is touching far more data than it needs.

Only then change something, and change one thing at a time. Add the index, refresh statistics, or rewrite the predicate, and re-measure with the same method. Its purpose is to catch defects the author cannot see, to spread knowledge of the codebase, and to keep the design coherent over time. The most useful reviews are prompt and small. A change of two hundred lines gets genuine scrutiny; a change of two thousand gets skimmed and rubber-stamped, which is worse than no review at all because it manufactures false confidence. Authors help by splitting work into reviewable units and by writing a description that explains why the change exists, not merely what it does.

Good comments distinguish severity. A reviewer who marks blocking correctness concerns separately from optional suggestions lets the author act without guessing. Comments should point at the specific failure a reader can imagine, ideally with the input that triggers it, rather than gesturing at vague unease. Questions are often better than assertions, since the author usually knows constraints the reviewer does not.

Finally, tone compounds over hundreds of reviews. Critique aimed at the code rather than the person, acknowledgment of what was done well, and a willingness to approve once the substantive issues are resolved keep the practice sustainable. [{"role": "user", "content": "Give me a thorough, multi-paragraph explanation of how compound interest works, with a worked example."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Compound interest is interest calculated on both the original principal and on the interest that has already been added to it. Simple interest pays out on the principal alone, so it grows in a straight line. Compounding folds each payment back into the balance, so the base on which interest is calculated keeps expanding, and growth curves upward.

The mechanics depend on the compounding frequency. If a balance compounds annually, interest is added once a year. If it compounds monthly, one twelfth of the annual rate is applied twelve times, and each application works on a slightly larger balance than the last. More frequent compounding therefore yields slightly more over the same period at the same nominal rate.

A worked example makes this concrete. Put $10,000 into an account paying 6% compounded annually. After year one you have $10,600. In year two, the 6% applies to $10,600 rather than $10,000, giving $11,236, so you earned $636 instead of $600. After ten years the balance reaches about $17,908, whereas simple interest would have produced only $16,000. The $1,908 difference is entirely interest earned on prior interest, and that gap widens sharply the longer the money is left alone."}]
